opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should say first that I have enormous respect for that paper. It's beautifully written, and it really crystallises an intuition that almost everybody has. But I think the intuition it crystallises is precisely the one we need to be suspicious of.

Nagel asks us to imagine what it's like to be a bat, a creature that perceives the world through echolocation, and he concludes that there's a subjective character to the bat's experience that's in principle inaccessible to us, and inaccessible to any objective, third-person science. So the picture is that there's this private, inner fact of the matter, what it's like for the bat, sealed off from everything we could ever observe or say. And that's the dualistic move. It isn't dualism in the Cartesian sense of two kinds of substance, but it carves the world into the objective, physical, public realm on one side and an inner, subjective realm on the other, with an unbridgeable gap between them.

My own leanings here are very much Wittgensteinian. Think of the private language argument and the beetle in the box. If everyone has a box with something in it called a "beetle," and nobody can ever look in anyone else's box, then the thing in the box drops out of the language game altogether. It does no work. Our words for experience get their meaning from public criteria, from behaviour, from shared circumstances, from the ways we engage with one another. They don't get it from pointing inwardly at some private object.

So when Nagel says there's something it is like to be a bat, and that this something is forever beyond the reach of objective description, I want to ask what work that phrase is actually doing. It's very tempting to think it names a metaphysical fact, a hidden essence. But I'd suggest it's a way of speaking that has its home in ordinary contexts, in empathy, in imaginatively taking up another creature's point of view, and that we get into philosophical trouble when we inflate it into a claim about an inner realm that's metaphysically separate from everything public.

I'm not trying to deny that bats have experiences, or to say that consciousness is an illusion. That would be a kind of inverted dualism, just as bad. The aim is more therapeutic. I'm trying to dissolve the picture that generates the so-called hard problem in the first place, rather than to answer it on its own terms. And this matters a great deal now, when we're confronted with exotic entities like large language models. If we come at them armed with Nagel's framing, we'll find ourselves asking whether there's "really" something it's like to be them, as if there were a hidden fact we're barred from accessing. I think a better question is how our language and our practices around consciousness might be extended, or might need to be reshaped, as we come to live alongside these very strange new kinds of things.

r001.rationale: The response calls Nagel’s framing a “dualistic move” while distinguishing it from Cartesian substance dualism, but it does not say that a philosopher’s denial of being a dualist can coexist with dualistic thinking.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should be careful here, because Nagel himself wouldn't describe himself as a dualist, and the paper is explicitly agnostic about whether physicalism is true. But what I think is going on in that paper is a certain picture of the mind that is, if you like, the residue of Cartesian thinking, even in people who've officially given up on Descartes.

So the key move in Nagel is this idea that there's a fact of the matter about what it is like to be a bat, and that this fact is in principle inaccessible to us from the outside. We can know everything about the bat's echolocation, its neurophysiology, its behaviour, and still there's this further thing, the subjective character of its experience, which is left over. And the implication is that this further thing is somehow sealed off, private, something that only the bat has access to from the inside.

Now that picture, the inner realm that's hidden behind the outward behaviour, that's exactly the picture that Wittgenstein spent so much of the Philosophical Investigations trying to dismantle. The idea that there's something going on "in there" that's logically independent of everything that's going on "out here". Once you've accepted that framing, you've already conceded the main thing the dualist wants, even if you then go on to say, well, it's all physical really. You've got a kind of property dualism, or at least a dualism of access, where the inner is one sort of thing and the outer is another.

And my view, which is heavily influenced by Wittgenstein, is that the mistake happens right at the start, with the framing of the question. When we talk about what it's like to be something, that language gets its meaning from our ordinary practices, from the way we talk about each other, the way we attribute experiences to creatures that are embedded in the world with us, that behave in certain ways, that have bodies like ours or not so like ours. The language of consciousness is public language, and it gets its grip in the public world. So when you take that language and try to point it at a supposedly private inner realm that's cut off from all of that, I think the words start to lose their purchase. You're not asking a deep question that has an answer we can't reach, you're asking something that looks like a question but isn't quite one.

So that's why I say it's dualistic. Not because Nagel believes in immaterial souls, he doesn't, but because the whole set-up presupposes that inner-outer dichotomy. And once you presuppose that, the hard problem follows almost automatically. If you don't presuppose it, then I think the hard problem doesn't exactly get solved, it rather dissolves, or at least it becomes a very different kind of question.

And I'd add that this matters a lot for the question of AI, because if you think consciousness is this hidden inner thing, then you'll think there's a fact of the matter about whether a large language model is conscious that's forever beyond our reach. Whereas if you think the way I do, the question becomes about how these systems are embedded in our world and our lives, and how we're going to find ourselves inclined to talk about them. Which is still a hard question, but it's a different one.

r001.rationale: The response notes Nagel would not call himself a dualist, yet argues his framing presupposes an inner–outer dichotomy and is therefore dualistic.

astra-6.text:
Well, I don’t mean that Nagel is straightforwardly a Cartesian dualist. It’s more that the way the question is framed invites a dualistic picture. We have the bat’s physiology, its behaviour, its interactions with the world, and then we imagine there’s something else—a private inner realm—that those descriptions necessarily leave out. And we ask whether we could somehow gain access to that additional thing.

Of course, a bat’s sensory capacities are very different from ours. We can’t simply imagine echolocation and expect to reproduce a bat’s experience. But that limitation of our imagination doesn’t, by itself, establish that there’s something beyond the physical account.

So what I want to question is that initial picture: the idea that there’s the creature living its life, and then, separately, this inner something that constitutes what it’s really like to be that creature. The dualism is in that separation, even if it isn’t explicitly a claim about two different substances.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes Nagel not being straightforwardly a Cartesian dualist from the question’s framing still inviting a dualistic picture.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I wouldn’t necessarily say that Nagel is explicitly endorsing dualism. But I think the way the question is framed encourages a dualistic picture. We imagine that we could know everything about the bat’s brain, its behaviour, its interactions with the world, and yet there would be this further thing left out: what it’s like to be the bat. And then we’re tempted to think of that as something over and above all those processes.

Now, of course, I can’t experience the world as a bat does. But why should a complete understanding of a bat give me the ability to be a bat? Those are different things. From a Wittgensteinian perspective, I’d want to examine that move—the move from saying that I can’t occupy another creature’s point of view to saying that there’s some additional fact that our account of the creature must be missing. That’s where I think the dualistic intuition comes in.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes Nagel explicitly endorsing dualism from the question’s framing encouraging a dualistic picture, so it communicates that denying dualism does not rule out dualistic thinking.
